Mayr's equation

Herbert Mayr's group at LMU Munich measured the rates of thousands of reactions between nucleophiles and electrophiles and found that one short equation describes them, at 20 °C:

log k = sN (N + E)log k₂₀ °C, with k the second-order rate constant in M⁻¹ s⁻¹

N
the nucleophilicity of the nucleophile. It belongs to the nucleophile in one solvent: the same anion has different N values in water and in DMSO.
sN
the sensitivity of that nucleophile, the slope of its line below. Most values lie between about 0.5 and 1.2.
E
the electrophilicity of the electrophile, treated as independent of the solvent.

Because log k = 0 when E = −N, a nucleophile's N is minus the E of an electrophile it attacks with k = 1 M⁻¹ s⁻¹. The parameters of a few hundred electrophiles and more than a thousand nucleophiles are collected in Mayr's Database of Reactivity Parameters, where every card in this app links to its entry.

How N, sN and E are measured

Mayr and Patz fixed the scales in 1994 with two definitions: E = 0 for the bis(4-methoxyphenyl)methylium ion, and sN = 1 for 2-methylpent-1-ene. Benzhydrylium ions Ar₂CH⁺ and quinone methides, whose reactivity can be tuned over a wide range by changing their substituents, became the reference electrophiles.

  1. A new nucleophile is combined with several reference electrophiles of known E, and each rate constant k is measured, usually by following the coloured electrophile by UV–vis spectroscopy.
  2. Plotting log k against E gives a straight line. Its slope is sN, and the E where it crosses log k = 0 is −N.
  3. A new electrophile is measured the other way round, against reference nucleophiles of known N and sN: each gives E = log k / sN − N, and the values are averaged.

In 2012 the whole benzhydrylium data set was refitted (Ammer, Nolte and Mayr); the database, and this app, use the current values.

Reading the numbers

  • The −5 rule of thumb. When sN is ignored, a pair reacts at room temperature if N + E > −5. That is the rule behind Reacting?; the feedback then works out log k with sN.
  • The fast end. Near k = 10⁹–10¹⁰ M⁻¹ s⁻¹ reactions become diffusion-controlled: every encounter reacts, the equation stops working (above about 10⁸) and selectivity is lost.
  • One solvent at a time. N depends strongly on the solvent, especially for anions, which water and alcohols solvate by hydrogen bonding. The nitromethane anion has N = 20.71 in DMSO but 12.06 in water. Rank therefore only compares nucleophiles measured in the same solvent; E values can be compared across all sets.
  • Crossing lines. Two nucleophiles with different sN can swap order depending on the electrophile, as two lines in the chart above can cross. Ranking by N alone, as in Rank, is Mayr's own first approximation.
  • Where the equation works. It was built for reactions in which one new bond forms and steric effects are small. Bulky partners (a trityl cation with a hindered amine) and SN2 reactions at alkyl halides are less well described.

Which atom reacts

Many nucleophiles have more than one nucleophilic atom (enolates, cyanide, thiocyanate, pyridones, amino alcohols), and many electrophiles more than one electrophilic atom (enones, molecules with two carbonyl groups). For ambident reactivity Mayr, Breugst and Ofial (2011) replaced the hard and soft acids and bases (HSAB) rule with three questions:

  1. Is the reaction reversible? Then the more stable product wins (thermodynamic control): N-attack of thiocyanate, C-alkylation of enamines.
  2. If not, which site is faster? Marcus theory splits the barrier into an intrinsic part and the reaction's driving force. Reactions with high intrinsic barriers, such as SN2 at carbon, follow the more stable product even under kinetic control: enolates are C-alkylated by alkyl halides.
  3. Is it diffusion-controlled? Then every encounter reacts and there is no selectivity: very reactive carbocations attack cyanide at both ends.

For regioselectivity in addition, substitution and elimination reactions, the same two ideas, the stability of the cation, anion or radical formed and kinetic against thermodynamic control, explain most of the questions in the Regioselectivity tab. Each answer comes with a short reason.

Computed indices: ω and N from orbital energies

Mayr's parameters are measured. Computational chemists often estimate reactivity instead from a single calculation per molecule, with the conceptual DFT indices. With Koopmans' approximation, the ionisation energy is I ≈ −εHOMO and the electron affinity A ≈ −εLUMO, and:

μ = (εHOMO + εLUMO) / 2
electronic chemical potential: how strongly the molecule holds on to its electrons (Parr and Pearson 1983).
η = εLUMO − εHOMO
chemical hardness: resistance to charge transfer. Some authors include a factor ½; Domingo's scales below leave it out.
ω = μ² / (2η)
global electrophilicity index: the energy gained when the molecule takes up as much electron density from its surroundings as it can (Parr, von Szentpály and Liu 1999).
N = εHOMO(Nu) − εHOMO(TCE)
Domingo's nucleophilicity index, measured from the HOMO of tetracyanoethylene computed at the same level of theory (B3LYP/6-31G(d) in the published scales), so that it is positive for nearly all nucleophiles (Domingo, Chamorro and Pérez 2008).
Class (Domingo 2016)Electrophiles, ωNucleophiles, N
Strong> 1.5 eV> 3.0 eV
Moderate0.8–1.5 eV2.0–3.0 eV
Marginal< 0.8 eV< 2.0 eV

The inverse of the electrophilicity, 1/ω, is sometimes used as a nucleophilicity index. It follows nucleophilicity only within limited series of molecules (it fails, for example, for captodative ethylenes), so the thresholds above are for Domingo's N.

Local versions: which atom

Condensed Fukui functions split a global index over the atoms. From the atomic charges qk of the molecule with N, N+1 and N−1 electrons, all at the neutral geometry: fk⁺ = qk(N) − qk(N+1) marks the atoms that nucleophiles attack, and fk⁻ = qk(N−1) − qk(N) the atoms that attack electrophiles (Yang and Mortier 1986). Domingo's Parr functions use the atomic spin densities of the radical anion (Pk⁺) and radical cation (Pk⁻) instead, giving local indices ωk = ω·Pk⁺ and Nk = N·Pk⁻.

How the two kinds of number relate

The conceptual DFT indices describe one isolated molecule from one calculation; Mayr's parameters are rate constants measured in solution, with solvation and steric effects included. They tend to agree within a family of similar molecules, but they are not on the same scale: Mayr's N and Domingo's N share a letter and nothing else.

Radical philicity

Radicals lack a full octet, but being "electron deficient" does not make them electrophiles. What decides is the energy of the singly occupied orbital (SOMO). Groups that push electron density into it raise it, and the radical is nucleophilic: it reacts fastest with electron-poor partners. Groups that pull density out of it lower it, and the radical is electrophilic (Parsaee and co-workers 2021).

Raise the SOMO: nucleophilic
alkyl groups (hyperconjugation); a lone pair next to the radical centre (α-O, α-N, α-S, and the C=O of an acyl radical); a radical on an atom less electronegative than carbon (B, Si).
Lower the SOMO: electrophilic
π acceptors such as CO₂R and CN (one is enough for a primary radical, a secondary or tertiary one needs two); fluorines (•CF₃); more s character (aryl, vinyl and alkynyl radicals); a radical on an atom more electronegative than carbon (O, N, S, Cl, Br).

Some radicals are ambiphilic, such as methyl, aryl and •CF₃: they react with both kinds of partner, and the Radicals tab asks how they usually react. Polarity also steers hydrogen-atom transfer (HAT): an electrophilic radical (t-BuO•, Cl•, an aminium radical cation) takes the electron-rich, "hydridic" C–H next to O or N, whereas a nucleophilic one prefers electron-poor C–H bonds. Choosing the HAT catalyst for this is called polarity-reversal catalysis.

Is there a Mayr scale for radicals?

Not one with measured N and E values that add up in log k = sN(N + E). Radical additions are fast, and their rates depend on polar and enthalpy effects together: Fischer and Radom described them with the radical's ionisation energy, its electron affinity and the reaction enthalpy (2001), and Héberger and Lopata fitted philicity parameters to measured addition rates (1998). Computed scales exist: De Vleeschouwer, De Proft and co-workers gave electrophilicity and nucleophilicity indices for radicals from vertical ionisation energies and electron affinities, each computed as an energy difference between the radical and its cation or anion (2007). For an open-shell molecule the orbital-energy shortcut of the previous section does not give a clean IE or EA, which is why they used energy differences.

Redox potentials

A redox potential belongs to a couple, the oxidised and reduced forms of one species: Ox + e⁻ ⇌ Red. It is always written as a reduction potential, even when the reaction of interest is an oxidation, so an amine's card reads E(R₃N•⁺/R₃N). The more positive E, the more strongly Ox pulls in an electron (a strong oxidant); the more negative E, the more readily Red gives one away (a strong reductant).

E½
the half-wave potential of a reversible couple in cyclic voltammetry, the mean of the two peak potentials. It is close to the formal potential, the thermodynamic value.
Eₚ and Eₚ/₂
for an irreversible wave, when the radical ion falls apart before it can be turned back, only the peak potential Eₚ can be read, and it overshoots. Roth, Romero and Nicewicz (2016) measured the half-peak potential Eₚ/₂ for about 180 substrates under one set of conditions: for mesitylene Eₚ/₂ = +2.07 V, close to the true +2.05 V, whereas Eₚ is +2.3 V.
E°
the standard potential, tabulated for couples in water against the standard hydrogen electrode.

Reference electrodes

Potentials are differences, so each needs its reference. In water it is the standard hydrogen electrode (SHE, 0 V by definition); the saturated calomel electrode (SCE) sits at +0.241 V against it. Most photoredox papers report V vs SCE in acetonitrile. For organic solvents IUPAC recommends the ferrocenium/ferrocene couple measured in the same solution, Fc⁺/Fc, whose potential against SCE depends on the solvent:

SolventE½(Fc⁺/Fc) vs SCE
MeCN+0.40 V
CH₂Cl₂+0.46 V
DMF+0.45 V
THF+0.56 V

The Potentials vs option converts with these offsets (Connelly and Geiger 1996): E vs Fc⁺/Fc = E vs SCE − offset. Aqueous potentials stay against SHE.

How far to trust the numbers

  • Reversible couples, such as the photocatalysts' ground states, are reproducible to a few hundredths of a volt; the same catalyst can still differ by about 0.1 V between papers (Ru(bpy)₃³⁺/²⁺: +1.29 V in MacMillan's table, Eₚ/₂ = +1.39 V in Nicewicz's).
  • Irreversible reductions of alkyl halides depend strongly on how they are measured: CF₃I is quoted at −1.22 and −1.52 V vs SCE, α-bromoacetophenone at −0.49 and −1.46 V. Treat such values as rough guides.
  • Comparing potentials measured in different solvents adds about 0.1 V of uncertainty.

Excited states

Light gives the catalyst its excitation energy E₀,₀ (in eV), which makes it both a better donor and a better acceptor (the Rehm–Weller approximation, ignoring small Coulomb terms):

E(PC⁺/PC*) ≈ E(PC⁺/PC) − E₀,₀the excited state as a reductant

E(PC*/PC⁻) ≈ E(PC/PC⁻) + E₀,₀the excited state as an oxidant

For Ru(bpy)₃²⁺: +1.29 − 2.10 = −0.81 V and −1.33 + 2.10 = +0.77 V, with E₀,₀ ≈ 2.1 eV, close to the energy of its 615 nm emission (2.0 eV).

Will the electron move?

For an electron going from a donor D to an acceptor A, in eV:

ΔGET ≈ E(D•⁺/D) − E(A/A•⁻)negative: downhill, the transfer can happen

That is the comparison behind Reacting? in its Electron transfer mode, and behind the Photoredox tab. A downhill step is necessary but not sufficient: the partners must also meet within the excited state's lifetime (about 1 µs for *Ru(bpy)₃²⁺).

Potentials from calculations

A reduction potential measures a free-energy difference: E = −ΔGred/(nF) − Eabs(ref), where ΔGred is the free energy of Ox + e⁻ → Red in solution and Eabs the absolute potential of the reference electrode (about 4.4 V for the SHE; values from 4.28 to 4.44 V are in use). It is related to, but not the same as, the ionisation energy and electron affinity of the conceptual DFT section: those are for the isolated molecule, while the potential includes the very different solvation of the neutral and the ion. Roth, Romero and Nicewicz computed their whole data set with B3LYP and M06-2X/6-31+G(d,p) and CPCM acetonitrile, from the free energies of the two forms; the calculated values followed the measured ones with R² = 0.96–0.97.

Photoredox cycles

A photocatalyst absorbs visible light and, in its long-lived excited state, gives or takes one electron. Two cycles return it to the ground state (Prier, Rankic and MacMillan 2013):

Oxidative quenching
the excited catalyst gives an electron to an acceptor A, which needs E(PC⁺/PC*) below E(A/A•⁻). The oxidised catalyst PC⁺ then takes an electron from a donor D, which needs E(PC⁺/PC) above E(D•⁺/D). Typical oxidative quenchers: viologens, aryldiazonium salts, polyhalomethanes, electron-poor arenes, persulfate.
Reductive quenching
the excited catalyst takes an electron from a donor D, which needs E(PC*/PC⁻) above E(D•⁺/D). The reduced catalyst PC⁻ then gives it to an acceptor A, which needs E(PC/PC⁻) below E(A/A•⁻). Typical reductive quenchers: tertiary amines, Hantzsch esters, carboxylates, borates.

Each catalyst card in the Redox sets gives these four potentials. Changing the ligands moves them together: electron-poor ligands (bpz, dF(CF₃)ppy) shift every potential positive and give strong excited-state oxidants; electron-rich cyclometalated ligands (ppy) give strong reductants, as in fac-Ir(ppy)₃ (−1.73 V).

Thermodynamics says which cycles are possible; when both are, the partner that meets the excited state first decides. Stern–Volmer experiments measure this: the emission fades as an added quencher takes the excited state away, and only the partners that quench it can start the cycle. Some catalysts do neither: they pass on their excitation energy to a partner with a lower triplet energy (energy transfer), and no electron moves.

The Photoredox tab asks three kinds of question: which cycle a published reaction uses, which catalyst can do both steps for a given donor and acceptor, and which partner can bring the catalyst back after the first step. The last two are generated from the potentials in the Redox sets; each step counts as possible when ΔGET is at least 0.1 eV downhill and impossible when it is at least 0.1 eV uphill.
